title: Samsung Galaxy A56 5G review: Great price, but the competition is better
text:
The Galaxy A56 5G was also a generally solid companion as I worked my way around Sacramento ahead of running the California International Marathon. I had no problems trusting it for navigation through the downtown area and around the Sacramento State campus, relying on Samsung’s large battery and sharp display to keep me generally on the right track, despite my occasional side quests.

The phone also had the honor of serving alongside the TCL NXTPAPER 60 Ultra as my at-home entertainment over the Christmas holidays. This largely meant bingeing the entire final season of Stranger Things because I’m locked out of my parents’ Netflix whenever I’m not under their roof, as well as streaming an audiobook in half-hour chunks whenever I needed some quiet while visiting relatives.

...

When we flip over to the GPU side of our gauntlet, the Galaxy A56 5G falls back down to its place at the bottom of the pile. Yes, it still beats the previous Galaxy A55 5G across all 20 runs of the test, but that’s about it. The mid-ranger still starts (and finishes) below its rivals from Google and OnePlus, making it an option for light gaming at best. To Samsung’s credit, the Galaxy A56 boasts some of the best stability of the phones tested, barely tailing off despite 20 minutes of testing. However, this raises the question: would you rather burn twice as bright or twice as long?

I’ve also noticed one or two stumbles where I didn’t expect them, lending to my worries about sustained performance. I booted up Pokémon TCG Pocket once again over the holidays, purely because I needed a way to waste time, and found that the Galaxy A56 could merely stumble through my power needs. Then again, it’s been a while since I’ve played, so I did start with a pretty hefty update.

I'd trade some of the Galaxy A56 5G's battery life for a bit more power, no question.

Anyway, I think my answer on power usage is somewhere in between — I’d happily burn a little brighter even if I couldn’t run for as long. Unfortunately, I found myself thinking that quite a lot during my time with the Galaxy A56. It’s a fine phone, and it cruises through the basics just as easily as you’d expect, but it doesn’t feel as polished as Google’s Pixel 9a, and the fall-off from the Galaxy S25 FE’s Exynos 2400 chipset is noticeable.

In fact, I’d much rather spend the money to put either of those phones in my pocket, preferring their power, AI features, and longevity over the course of their seven years of updates, which makes the extra cost of Samsung’s sub-flagship hardly noticeable. If you really can’t work the additional $150 or so for the Galaxy S25 FE into your budget, though, the Galaxy A56 is good in a pinch.

It’s a more than decent battery performer, too, which has helped to ease some of my stress. I didn’t have the highest of hopes for Samsung’s combination of yet another 5,000mAh battery with its Exynos 1580 chipset, yet the Galaxy A56 came through. It lasted longer in our controlled testing than Google’s Pixel 9a — a phone that the company boasted had its best battery on a Pixel. Samsung edged the mid-ranger in almost every leg, and when it fell behind, the margins were pretty tight.

Likewise, I found myself able to push through at least a day and a half between charges, which was especially helpful in California. Between the long days of adventuring and the jet lag, I fell asleep more than once before I was ready to. That meant forgetting to charge my Galaxy A56 and starting the next day with a partially charged cell. Conveniently, though, the Galaxy A56 now supports the same 45W wired charging as Samsung’s top-tier Galaxy flagships.

Interestingly, though, that 45W support doesn’t actually translate to charging as fast as the Galaxy S25 Ultra. Instead, the Galaxy A56 5G turns in a performance that lasts about 75 minutes from empty to full, which is an improvement nevertheless. It’s almost perfectly centered between the Moto G Stylus (2025) and the Pixel 9a, which makes sense, as the former supports 68W charging while the latter is capped at 23W.

Samsung is also hoping you’ll be happy with its wired charging upgrade, as there’s, well, no wireless charging to tap into. Both of its rivals above offer wireless speeds, but Samsung would rather take that odd step backwards. Anyway, you’ll need a capable 45W charger if you want to spend as little time tethered to power as possible, so you might want to check out a few of our favorite chargers.

title: 5 Midrange Phones With Better Battery Life Than ... - BGR
text:
This phone ships with a 5,000 mAh battery, and according to independent tests by GSMArena, it can last up to 12 hours and 8 minutes on a single charge in combined use, involving calling, browsing the web, streaming video, and gaming. As expected, the actual battery life will vary depending on your usage. Regardless, there are midrange phones with far better battery life than what the Galaxy A56 offers.

...

In GSMArena's tests, the phone lasted for 13 hours and 59 minutes in combined use, nearly two hours more than the Galaxy A56. Individually, the Galaxy A57 lasted up to 23 hours and 12 minutes for video streaming, 13 hours and 32 minutes for web browsing, 23 hours and 15 minutes for calls, and 7 hours and 12 minutes for gaming. And once you run out of charge, recharging the A57 shouldn't take long, as it supports 45 W wired charging. You can buy the Samsung Galaxy A57 on Amazon or Best Buy starting at $550.

...

## How we selected these midrange phones

We used GSMArena's battery life test data to determine the battery life of the Samsung Galaxy A56. The Galaxy A56 lasted for 12 hours and 8 minutes in the site's battery life tests, and we relied on this as our baseline figure for comparison. With this figure, our job was to find phones that are not only midrange but also offer longer screen time than Samsung's phone in GSMArena's tests. For context, the site's battery life test involves a mixture of four different tests: calling, web browsing, gaming, and streaming video. 

The combined results from the four tests are used to calculate the site's so-called Active Use Score, which we used as a guideline to determine the A56's baseline battery life. All the phones we've listed have an MSRP that falls between $350 and $650, which is the range we used to define a midrange phone in this article. All the phones we've recommended in this article cost anywhere within that range. There are many more midrange phones that beat the Galaxy A56 in battery life per GSMArena's tests, but we only selected models that are officially sold in the U.S.

title: Samsung Galaxy A56 review: Lab tests - display, battery ...
text:
### Battery life

The Galaxy A56 runs on the same 5,000 mAh battery as last year but gets a slightly more powerful and, thus, potentially more power-hungry Exynos 1580 SoC. The phone also has a bit larger display and the battery endurance results reflect the changes.

The A56 has a slightly lower Active Use Score of 12:08 compared to last year by posting lower gaming and video playback runtimes. The web browsing score goes up a little, though.

In the context of other similarly priced phones, the A56 is just about average. For example, the Xiaomi 14T and the Motorola Edge 50 Pro sit lower than the A56, while the OnePlus Nord 4 and the Nothing Phone (3a) Pro edge out Samsung's offering.

### Charging speed

When it comes to charging speed, the Galaxy A56 offers an upgrade - 45W fast charging over Power Delivery with Samsung's PPS. We tested the phone with a 45W Samsung charger and got 1 hour and 13 minutes from 0 to 100%. Surprisingly, that's slower than last year's A55 to get to full, but the A56 is considerably faster at the 15 and 30-minute marks. You get 65% of the charge back in the first 30 minutes.

But compared to the competition, the A56 is behind the curve. There are a handful of alternatives that get close to the 100W mark or even go beyond, like the Motorola Edge 50 Pro and the OnePlus Nord 4.

text:
### Battery life

Our new battery benchmark uses PCMark for Android’s Work 3.0 Battery Life test to determine a modern Android-based smartphone's battery uptime in minutes. This controlled benchmark simulates real-world usage with a combination of both web and social media browsing, video and photo editing, parsing data with various file formats, writing (on documents), and more.

Battery life, on the other hand, is quite good. The 5,000mAh Galaxy A56 inches ahead most competitors. This phone can last a whole day if you don't play any games or binge-watch too many videos on it.

Charging speeds are also quick, with a 45W wired charge taking just 27 minutes to reach 50% from 0%. Speeds do slow down considerably after that, with the phone taking a total of 75 minutes to reach 100%.

...

Therefore, the only group it appeals to is users who want to be in Samsung's ecosystem and are constantly in need of extended battery life.

...

That’s not to say that everything about this phone is bad. If your needs are not exceptional (jumping between watching shopping livestreams, getting enraged on social media, and mindlessly browsing through your messages and calls), the Galaxy A56 still does all these well enough. Unfortunately, it's unlikely to find people who don't need a phone for work these days, too.

title: Samsung Galaxy A56 Review | Detailed Review after 6 Months
text: [Music] The Samsung Galaxy A56 is the latest addition to the hugely popular A50 series. With these phones, you can generally expect a premium build, great software experience, and long-lasting battery for a reasonable price. So, does the A56 live up to these expectations? And what kind of improvements does it get over last year's A55? Well, that's exactly what we'll try to find out in this detailed review of the Galaxy A56 after over 6 months of use. The Galaxy A56 has a different camera pump design instead of Samsung's typical triple camera ring design. This looks quite nice in my opinion. The dual finished frame is the highlight for me. It makes this phone look very premium. Compared to the A55, the A56 is 15 g lighter and 0.8 mm thinner, making it feel a lot better in hand. In terms of weight distribution, it is perfectly balanced, which is great. The build quality is also top-notch with Gorilla Glass Victus Plus on both the front and back. And this phone also gets an IP67 rating for protection against dust and water, which is always appreciated. So overall, this phone looks and feels very premium, and it's built to last with quality materials. This phone's display is quite nice. It's a big, bright, colorful, and smooth AMOLED display. It is also HDR certified and HDR content works well on both YouTube and Netflix. Even 4K 60fps HDR content works without any hiccups on this phone. It is certified for 1900 nits of peak HDR brightness and even manages to get around 1,400 nits of full screen brightness which is very impressive. However, in terms of PWM dimming, it disappoints as its frequency is very low by today's standards. Also, in terms of bezels, this phone feels quite outdated as even cheaper phones these days have thinner and symmetrical bezels. So, while the display quality is good, it is far from class leading. This phone has stereo speakers and they sound quite good. Here this audio sample. [Music] It is quite loud and distortion-free, but a little more bass would have made it even better. This is an audio recording test of the Galaxy A56, and this recorder app can do live transcription quite well. The earpiece is also very loud and clear and I had absolutely no issues handling calls with this phone. It supports wired audio over the USB type-C port and everything works as expected. Even in terms of wireless audio, everything works well. It supports Samsung's seamless codec and LDAC for lossless audio but misses out on the LHDC codec which is slightly disappointing. In terms of audio enhancement, there is support for Dolby Atmos as well as an equalizer. You can also tweak the music based on your hearing ability. So, in the audio department, I have hardly anything to complain about. The rear camera setup is pretty much the same as last year. However, the selfie camera has been upgraded even though its megapixel count has dropped from 32 MP to 12 MP. In terms of image quality, the primary camera produces greatl looking shots in most situations. Even in high dynamic range scenarios, this phone does a good job, though not the best. In indoor conditions, the camera balances outside light and indoor artificial lights quite well. Even in less than ideal lighting conditions, this phone does a good job in terms of white balance and exposure. The ultra wide camera generally maintains good color parity with the primary camera. It is one of the better ultra wide cameras in its price range. However, it still has limitations here. The ultra wide camera couldn't handle the dynamic range as well as the primary camera did. Also, it has a significant amount of edge distortion, which can sometimes ruin the entire photo. In low light, the ultra wide camera actually impresses with results very close to the primary camera in terms of colors, exposure, and white balance. The dedicated 5 MP macro camera is decent, but it is absolutely unnecessary these days. In most situations, you'll be better off using the primary camera with digital zoom for better looking close-up shots. This primary camera can take decent looking shots up to 3x digital zoom, but beyond that, it becomes unusable. It also takes good portrait shots in 1x and 2x modes. If you want an even more zoomed-in portrait shot, just take a regular photo and then add the portrait effect later in the gallery. The upgraded selfie camera definitely takes greatl looking shots in good light, but in low light, the results are a bit too soft for my liking. This phone can record videos in 4K 30fps and you can switch between cameras while shooting. However, there is no zoom transition effect while switching cameras. It is very abrupt. In terms of digital zoom, it can go up to 10x magnification, but the quality gets really bad at that zoom level. Here you can see the stabilization, focus, and low light video test. The phone does well in both the stabilization and focus tests, though the low light video could have been better. This is a video sample from the selfie camera of the Galaxy A56, and it is being recorded at 4K 30fps. In terms of the camera UI, it is quite intuitive with all the controls close to the bottom. It even has several useful modes. However, it doesn't have portrait video mode and in the pro mode only the primary camera is supported. So, the camera setup is quite capable but for the price the competition is offering way more. The software experience is easily the best aspect of this phone. 1 UI7 based on Android 15 is what you get out of the box. This UI looks quite modern and also feels fun to use. It has several useful features like edge panels, live notifications, floating windows, as well as crazy customization options and top-notch security. It offers some useful AI features like object eraser, best face, AI select, as well as Google's AI features like Gemini and Circle to search. However, it doesn't have Samsung's advanced TI features like generative edit and sketch to image. What it has instead is a lot of bloatware out of the box. All of this can be easily removed, but I feel Samsung should stop including all this to maintain a premium user experience. Speaking of premium user experience, 6 years of update commitment for a mid-range phone is definitely best-in-class. This phone is powered by the Exynus 1580 chip. Also, you get to choose between 8 or 12 GB of RAM and 128 or 256GB of storage. In terms of performance, this chip scores much better than the A55, but it still lags behind the competition. Still, the best part about this chip is its sustained performance. You get very good stability, and the device temperature is also well within limits. In day-to-day usage, this level of performance is good enough and everything runs smoothly. However, it is definitely not meant for serious gaming. It can do stable 60fps with light games like PUBG and Call of Duty, but with heavy games like Genchin Impact and Car Street, it struggles to maintain a stable frame rate. At least we get support for bypass charging, which is always good to have. So, performance-wise, it is good enough for casual users, but definitely not meant for gamers. Battery size-wise, 5,000 mAh was considered good up to last year, but now it's way below par. Still, with a lightweight chip and great optimization, the battery life this phone provides is excellent. You can easily expect around 8 hours of screen on time. While you don't get a charger in the box, this phone at least supports 45 watt speed, which is an improvement over last year's 25 W. Still, it takes over an hour to fully charge this phone. The box barely contains anything. They should have at least included a basic charger in the box. The optical fingerprint scanner as well as face unlock both work well, but they are not best in class. Same goes for the haptic feedback as well. It is good but not great. In terms of sensors and connectivity, most of the things are covered here including NFC. However, I hear a lot of people being concerned about the reliability of the virtual proximity sensor. So, here is a demo. This is the Galaxy A56 and I am on a call. Now, let's see whether the proximity sensor works or not. As you can see, it is working fine. So, nothing to be concerned about. In terms of network features and 5G bands, all the important stuff is covered. However, there is a downgrade in terms of the SIM tray. It is no longer a hybrid SIM tray. So, unfortunately, no micro SD support in this phone, but at least there is eSIM support, which is good. All right, conclusion time. This phone, like all the A50 phones before this, continues to deliver on design, software, and battery. This year, it has much better inhand field, and even as a content consumption device, it is pretty good. But when it comes to raw performance or cameras, this phone is definitely lagging behind the competition. While the pricing has gone down since launch, it is still far from being value for money, at least in India. In Western countries, it is available for under $350, which is very reasonable. Again, in terms of competition, there is fierce competition in India. So, this phone is only for those who want a Samsung branded phone which looks premium and can work well and last long. However, in western countries where there isn't much competition, this phone becomes an excellent choice for a lot of people. All right, that's it for this video. Hope you enjoyed it and found it useful. Please like, comment, share, and subscribe to my channel down below. Thanks for watching.
